prompt.context: Our client is the largest European manufacturer of wind turbines (used to generate electricity by harnessing wind power). The client currently has production capability in the US and has elicited your help. This problem only concerns North American Operations. Wind energy is currently growing in China and the US. By 2009, there will be capacity issues in the US.
prompt.question: 1. Where should the client build its manufacturing plant? 2. How many plants should the client build?

clarifying_info.q: Can the client import turbines to the US instead of building a plant?
clarifying_info.a: Importing turbines to the US or Asia is impractical because each weighs 80 tons and there are import tariffs that add additional costs.

clarifying_info.q: What is the expected demand for the client's products when the plant comes online?
clarifying_info.a: The plant will be online by 2010. Expected demand for the client's products is 1,500 units, which represents 40% of the market.

clarifying_info.q: What is the market growth rate?
clarifying_info.a: Market growth for the next 5 years is 10% per year by volume.
There are 2 existing US manufacturers of wind turbines with one being the dominant player. There is no differentiation between the different products.

clarifying_info.q: What are the investment costs for the plant?
clarifying_info.a: A 1,500-unit plant would cost $40 million dollars investment ($30 million being the building). Each additional 500 units in capacity will increase the costs by $15M. We cannot build a plant with lower than 1,500 units capacity.

clarifying_info.q: What are the costs of building two plants versus one?
clarifying_info.a: If 2 plants were built, the additional operating costs would be $15M per year. The transportation savings would be $7M per year.

exhibits.title: Relative Effect of Plant Scale on Costs
exhibits.shows: A chart showing how cost per unit changes as annual plant capacity increases
exhibits.data: X-axis: Annual Plant Capacity (0 to 5,000 units); Y-axis: Cost Per Unit (approximately 10.95 to 11.45); the curve shows cost per unit decreasing as plant capacity increases (economies of scale)

framework: Part & Material Supply — assess infrastructure, labor, taxes, competition, and from where competitors currently source (mid-west heavy auto supply base)
Manufacturing — assembly is low-tech mechanical assembly; all engineering design is done in Europe; only one type of turbine slated for US production
Transport — finished turbines must be shipped by rail; locate plant near areas of heavy demand to reduce transportation costs
Installation — customers perform their own installation; client provides nominal support
Service — routine maintenance performed by independent licensed contractors (fragmented market, low barrier to entry)
Demand sizing and capacity planning — model 40% market share at 10% annual growth to project required capacity through 2017
Plant location — near but southwest of the mid-west supply base to balance supply sourcing and proximity to demand
Number of plants — compare total cost of one large plant vs. two smaller plants

questions.prompt: What factors should drive the location decision for the new plant?
questions.guidance: Candidate should structure location drivers across: (1) proximity to part/material supply — competitors source from the mid-west heavy auto supply base, so a mid-west or nearby location reduces inbound logistics costs; (2) proximity to customer demand — finished turbines must be shipped by rail so closeness to demand clusters reduces outbound cost; (3) labor, infrastructure, and tax environment; (4) ability to outsource manufacturing vs. build. Strong candidates note that assembly is low-tech and the main cost drivers are shipping and integrated supplier network.

questions.prompt: How many units will the client need to produce by 2017? Build the demand projection.
questions.guidance: Start from 2010 demand of 1,500 units (40% of 3,750 market). Apply 10% annual market growth holding share constant at 40%.

math.setup: 2010 client demand = 1,500 (40% of 3,750). Market grows 10%/year. Client share held constant at 40%.
steps: 2017: market 7,308, client 2,923 (~3,000 rounding up for capacity planning)
math.answer: By 2017 the client will need roughly 3,000 units of capacity (approximately double the 2010 level).

questions.prompt: Should the client build one plant or two? Compare the costs.
questions.guidance: Candidate should compare total cost of one 3,000-unit plant vs. two 1,500-unit plants over an ~8-year horizon. Key insight: operating cost penalty of two plants ($15M/yr) exceeds transportation savings ($7M/yr), so net annual cost of two plants is +$8M/yr. One large plant is cheaper overall.

math.setup: One plant at 3,000 units: base $40M + 3 increments of 500 units × $15M each. Two plants at 1,500 units each: 2 × $40M capex + net annual cost of ($15M - $7M) × 8 years.
steps: Two plants net annual operating premium: $15M - $7M = $8M/yr
Difference: $144M - $85M = $59M more expensive for two plants
math.answer: One plant at $85M total cost vs. two plants at $144M total cost. Build one plant.

questions.prompt: How does plant scale affect cost per unit? What does the exhibit show?
questions.guidance: The exhibit shows declining cost per unit as annual plant capacity increases — classic economies of scale. A larger single plant achieves lower per-unit cost than two smaller plants, further reinforcing the one-plant recommendation. Candidate should note this supports both the size decision (build to 3,000 units eventually) and the single-plant decision.

brainstorming.prompt: What risks or additional considerations should be assessed before finalizing the recommendation?

categories.name: Competitive response
ideas: Dominant US player may cut prices or expand capacity to defend share
Second US competitor may also expand, further pressuring margins
No product differentiation means competition is purely on price and service

categories.name: Demand risk
ideas: 10% market growth is an assumption — regulatory changes (e.g., wind energy subsidies) could accelerate or reverse growth
Client's 40% market share could erode if competitors respond aggressively
China growth opportunity — client could consider exporting turbines to China from the US plant

categories.name: Execution risk
ideas: Plant must be online by 2010 — tight construction timeline
Sourcing a suitable site near the mid-west supply base with rail access
Hiring and training local assembly workforce

categories.name: Financial risk
ideas: $85M capital commitment requires financing; assess client's balance sheet
Capacity added in 500-unit increments provides flexibility but requires phased investment decisions
If demand grows slower than 10%, plant will be underutilized

recommendation: Build one plant, located near but southwest of the mid-west supply base, sized initially at 1,500 units with modular expansion capability to reach 3,000 units by approximately 2017.

One plant costs $85M total versus $144M for two plants over an 8-year horizon — a $59M saving — because the operating cost penalty of running two facilities ($15M/yr) exceeds the transportation savings ($7M/yr).
risks: Competitive response from the dominant US player could erode the assumed 40% market share
Market growth may not sustain 10% per year if renewable energy subsidies change
Tight 2010 go-live timeline for plant construction
next_steps: Conduct site selection analysis in the mid-west / southwest corridor focusing on rail access and proximity to the auto-parts supply base
Assess competitive dynamics and stress-test market share assumption
Evaluate phased capacity expansion schedule to minimize upfront capital while meeting demand growth
Explore whether China export opportunity is viable as a second revenue stream
